THE HUMAN ATLASES · DEEP DIVE

Marco Polo: journey, cities and a difficult book

Marco Polo’s account opens a window onto a connected thirteenth-century world. Its place names range far beyond a personal itinerary: some passages report travel, others describe cities, repeat stories or organize information for readers. Follow the journey while keeping those different kinds of evidence in view.

1254–1324 CE, with mapped journey phases mainly 1271–1295 and the account’s composition around 1298. Dates and routes are approximate where the evidence is approximate.

The whole area in view

Mediterranean to East Asia and the Indian Ocean. Points distinguish reported journey stages, described cities and secondhand geography; Japan has no journey connection.

  1. Venice: departure with father and uncle

    1271 CE

    The prologue places Marco with Niccolò and Maffeo on the departure for Acre. Marco did not accompany their earlier Asian journey. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [1] [10]

    Map reference: 45.44°, 12.34°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  2. Acre: papal negotiations

    1271 CE

    The account brings the three Polos to Acre during preparations for travel east. The family’s movements around Acre include return visits; the point is not an exact dated arrival. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [1] [10]

    Map reference: 32.92°, 35.07°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  3. Ayas: Cilician gateway

    1271 CE; repeated departure preparations

    Ayas, called Laiazzo, appears in the departure sequence between Acre and inland Asia. The map simplifies repeated journeys between these ports. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [10]

    Map reference: 36.77°, 35.79°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  4. Mainland Hormuz: outward-journey reconstruction

    Within the outward journey, 1271–1275 CE

    Polo describes Curmos as a port receiving Indian merchandise. This is an approximate mainland old-Hormuz anchor near Minab, not the later island city. The book supplies no secure stop year. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [3] [10] [17]

    Map reference: 27.1°, 57.07°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  5. Kashgar: described in the eastward sequence

    Within the outward journey, 1271–1275 CE

    The Cascar chapter describes an oasis of gardens, crafts and merchants. A place in the book’s geographical sequence is not an independently dated personal visit. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [4]

    Map reference: 39.47°, 75.99°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  6. Shangdu: reported arrival at Kublai’s court

    About 1275 CE

    Shangdu is conventionally identified with the court reached near the end of the outward journey. The arrival year is a historical reconstruction; palace descriptions do not locate every movement of the Polos. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [5] [10] [14] [18]

    Map reference: 42.358°, 116.185°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  7. Khanbaliq: the court described in the book

    Reported Yuan years, approximately 1275–1292 CE

    The account describes Kublai’s winter court at Cambaluc, present-day Beijing. This broad narrative setting does not imply uninterrupted residence or confirm every claimed office. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [6] [13]

    Map reference: 39.9°, 116.4°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  8. Hangzhou: a detailed city description

    After the 1276 conquest, within the reported Yuan years

    Quinsai is identified as Hangzhou, whose waterways, markets and urban life receive extended treatment. No precise visit year is established here. Manuscript versions differ; the book’s impressive numbers are not used as a census. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [9]

    Map reference: 30.25°, 120.15°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  9. Quanzhou: reported embarkation for the return

    Approximately 1291–1292 CE

    The return is conventionally reconstructed as embarking at Quanzhou, the book’s Çaiton. The departure date is approximate. Independent port archaeology establishes the trading setting, not Polo’s individual presence. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [10] [7] [15] [16] [18]

    Map reference: 24.906°, 118.59°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  10. Northern Sumatra: a claimed weather delay

    Within the return voyage, about 1292–1293 CE

    In the Samarra chapter, Marco explicitly claims a five-month stay caused by bad weather. The kingdom’s exact identification and the travel chronology remain uncertain; this point represents northern Sumatra broadly. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [8] [10]

    Map reference: 5.15°, 97.2°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  11. Mainland Hormuz: reported sea-journey endpoint

    Approximately 1293–1295 CE; reconstructions differ

    The maritime return is reconstructed as reaching Hormuz before travel back toward the Mediterranean. The broad date is not a harbor log; old mainland Hormuz is represented approximately. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [10] [3] [17] [19]

    Map reference: 27.1°, 57.07°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  12. Trebizond: named on the homeward route

    Before the 1295 return to Venice

    The prologue names Trebizond among the stages of the return west. The text gives a sequence, not an exact arrival date. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [2]

    Map reference: 41°, 39.72°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  13. Constantinople: named on the homeward route

    Before the 1295 return to Venice

    Constantinople follows Trebizond in the prologue’s homeward sequence. This date window is inferred from the return narrative, not proof of continuous residence. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [2]

    Map reference: 41.01°, 28.97°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  14. Negroponte: a homeward stop

    Before the 1295 return to Venice

    The prologue lists Negroponte, the Venetian name associated with Euboea, before Venice. Chalkis is a regional harbor anchor; the text does not supply an exact landing location or day. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [2]

    Map reference: 38.46°, 23.6°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  15. Venice: the stated return

    1295 CE

    The prologue dates the family’s arrival back in Venice to 1295. Arrival is a biographical event, not a foundation or population estimate for Venice. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [2]

    Map reference: 45.44°, 12.34°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  16. Genoa: a book takes shape

    Approximately 1298–1299 CE

    Tradition places the production of Polo’s account with Rustichello during imprisonment in Genoa. This marks the account’s composition context, not another stop on the Asian journey; circumstances of capture remain debated. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [11] [10] [18]

    Map reference: 44.41°, 8.93°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

  17. Japan / Cipangu: described, not visited

    Account compiled about 1298 CE

    The book’s Cipangu material belongs to secondhand reporting about Japan. No Polo journey connection leads here. The date marks the account, and the regional anchor does not identify a landing or settlement. Coordinates are approximate locality anchors. [12] [11]

    Map reference: 37°, 138°. Approximate unless the source establishes a surveyed position.

Begin with the family, then the journey

Marco joined his father Niccolò and uncle Maffeo after their earlier visit to Asia. The opening chapter places the three together on the departure from Venice for Acre. Keeping the two family journeys separate prevents a common map error: Marco should not appear on his relatives’ earlier travels through the Black Sea and Central Asia. [1] [18]

The playable chronology uses a few broad phases. It gives room to the uncertain years between departure and arrival, rather than assigning an exact year to every town in a geographical description. A line shows the reconstructed connection; a point’s note explains whether it represents a visit claim, a described place or the later creation of the book. [10] [18]

Iranian ports and Central Asian oases

Hormuz mattered because it joined inland routes with Indian Ocean commerce. The book’s Curmos chapter lists goods brought by ships, making the port a useful reminder that land and sea routes worked together. The mapped site is old Hormuz on the mainland near Minab; the familiar later island city would give the journey the wrong geographical setting. [3] [17]

Kashgar appears in the book’s eastward geographical sequence as a place of cultivation, craft production and trade. Those observations make an oasis intelligible as a lived settlement. They do not supply a dated entry in a travel diary. Here its location supports a broad reconstruction without pretending to identify a particular caravan track or day of arrival. [4]

Courts were places with their own histories

Shangdu and Khanbaliq belonged to a world already organized around Mongol rule, Chinese cities and regional institutions. Shangdu’s archaeological remains include a planned city and waterworks; UNESCO dates its design to 1256. That history precedes the reported Polo arrival and should not be mistaken for an event created by the visitor. [20]

The account describes Kublai’s winter palace at Cambaluc, while the Shangdu chapter describes another court setting. Scholarship compares such passages with Yuan evidence about palaces and administration. Comparisons can test specific observations, but a convincing description does not independently establish every office, mission or year claimed for the author. [6] [5] [13]

Read the cities at street level

Hangzhou, called Quinsai, receives unusually extensive treatment: waterways, markets and public spaces matter as much as rulers. Ca’ Foscari’s critical commentary shows why versions matter: details differ between manuscript traditions and later editions. The map therefore records a described city in a broad period, and leaves out apparently precise population totals that cannot be treated as a modern census. [9]

Quanzhou supplies an independent material setting for maritime commerce. Its heritage landscape includes docks, bridges, religious places and production sites serving a wider hinterland. These remains establish the scale and organization of a port society during the Song–Yuan period; by themselves they cannot prove that a particular traveller stood at a particular dock. [15] [16]

A sea journey governed by weather

The Samarra passage is unusually personal: Marco claims a five-month weather delay. Its account of waiting contrasts with a smooth line drawn across a modern map. Northern Sumatra is shown as a regional anchor because the medieval kingdom’s precise identification is uncertain; the display does not turn the text’s duration into an invented calendar of sailing dates. [8]

The homeward prologue names Trebizond, Constantinople and Negroponte before placing the return to Venice in 1295. Those names support a sequence, while the spaces between them remain schematic. The maritime endpoint at Hormuz is dated broadly because published reconstructions differ. [2] [17] [19]

What did the writer actually see?

Japan is the clearest caution on this map. Polo’s Cipangu description is secondhand, and its geography and wealth claims require criticism. The marker represents a place described in the account around the time of composition. No journey line reaches it. [12]

The surviving work passed through different languages and manuscripts; its earliest version is lost. The Library of Congress describes a mixture of travel reporting, practical information, legend and hearsay. Reading it critically means asking about each passage’s genre and transmission, rather than choosing between believing everything and dismissing the whole account. [18] [11]

Objects can test context without identifying a traveller

An archaeological study by Lin Meicun and Ran Zhang reassessed a Chinese porcelain jar in Venice and related finds across the Indian Ocean. The authors argue that its date and distribution support an association with Polo’s era and journey. The association remains an interpretation: an object’s manufacture and movement do not automatically provide its owner’s itinerary. [19]

Use the linked institutional maps to examine the places behind the narrative. They map surviving heritage sites and their components, not thirteenth-century political borders or an exact Polo route. The paired Silk Roads guide widens the view to other documents and settlements across much longer periods. [14] [16]
